topics.title: How to negotiate anything
topics.dek: BATNA, anchors, interests over positions and the power of silence

slides.h: Know your walk-away before you sit down
slides.p: Your BATNA is your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you'll do if this falls through. The better it is, the calmer you are, and the other side can tell. Improve it before you negotiate (get a second offer, a second quote) and never reveal it if it's weak.

items: Walk if it's worse than the alternative

slides.h: Positions are what people say; interests are why
slides.p: 'I need $90,000' is a position. 'I need to cover the move and not take a pay cut' is an interest, and interests can be met in more than one way: a signing bonus, a review in six months, remote days. Ask 'what would that do for you?' until you hear the why.

The first number sets the range. Research shows final agreements land closer to whoever anchored. If you know the market, anchor first, high but defensible. If you don't, ask them to go first, and treat their number as information, not a ceiling.

marks: midpoint drifts toward the first number

slides.h: Find the zone, or there's no deal
slides.p: The ZOPA is the overlap between the most they'll pay and the least you'll take. If it exists, the negotiation is about where in it you land. If it doesn't, no technique will make it appear, and the best outcome is to find that out quickly and politely.

Splitting the difference leaves value on the table. Instead, give on what's cheap for you and valuable to them, and ask for what's cheap for them and valuable to you: delivery date for price, title for salary, a longer contract for a lower rate. Every concession should come with an 'if'.

items: 'If you can do X, I can do Y.'
Several issues on the table at once
Ask what matters most to them
Conceding one thing at a time for nothing

slides.p: After you state a number, stop talking. People fill silence by negotiating against themselves. When you hear an offer, pause, repeat the key figure back as a question ('Forty-two?'), and wait. Most of the time the next sentence improves it.

items: Stop. Count to five if you must.
Mirror their last words as a question

slides.h: Make it easy to say yes
slides.p: Give reasons ('because' raises compliance even for weak reasons), offer a choice between two acceptable options rather than yes or no, and let the other side save face. People agree to things they can explain to their boss. Help them write that explanation.

items: Leave them a way to say yes
Put it in writing the same day

slides.h: What to do at the end
slides.p: Summarise what was agreed, in writing, today. Confirm who does what by when. Thank them; you'll likely meet again. And if there's no deal, leave the door open: 'If anything changes on your side, call me.' A good no is worth more than a bad yes.

a: What you'll do if no agreement is reached
The midpoint of the two positions
quiz.why: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement. A strong one is the real source of calm and leverage.

quiz.q: Research on anchoring suggests final deals tend to land…
a: Closer to whoever named the first number
quiz.why: The first number frames the range. Anchor first when you know the market; otherwise treat their anchor as information.

a: The overlap between what you'll accept and what they'll pay
quiz.why: Zone Of Possible Agreement. If it doesn't exist, no technique creates it; finding out fast is the win.

take: Improve your alternative before you negotiate; it's your real leverage.
Ask for the interest behind the position; trade across issues instead of splitting.
Anchor first when informed, then stop talking.

topics.title: How to remember anything
topics.dek: The forgetting curve, spaced repetition, testing yourself and sleep

slides.h: You forget most of it within a day
slides.p: In the 1880s Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised nonsense syllables and tested himself over time. He found a steep curve: most of what's learned once is gone within a day or two unless it is revisited. The shape has been replicated many times since.

Reviewing just as you're about to forget resets the curve higher and makes the next decline slower. Four or five well-timed reviews can carry something for years. That's spaced repetition, and it beats cramming by a wide margin for the same total time.

Review after about a day, then three days, then a week, then two, then a month, stretching each gap when you recall it easily and shrinking it when you don't. Apps like Anki do the scheduling; an index-card box with five slots does it on paper.

Pulling something out of memory strengthens it far more than putting it in again. Students who read a passage once and then tested themselves remembered more a week later than students who reread it four times, even though the rereaders felt more confident. Close the book and recall.

Practising one skill in a block feels productive; mixing related skills (interleaving) feels harder and works better, because you have to choose the method each time, which is what the exam or real life demands. Shuffle the problem types, the chord changes, the vocabulary themes.

Isolated facts slip; connected ones stick. Explain the idea to someone else in your own words, ask 'why is that true?', attach it to something you already know, or turn it into an image. The weirder and more vivid the image, the better memory likes it.

Memory athletes place items along a route they know, the rooms of a childhood home, and walk it to recall them in order. The technique is ancient and works because spatial memory is excellent. Twenty grocery items in a palace beat twenty on a list, for most people, on the first try.

items: Pick a route you know cold
Put one item at each stop as a vivid scene
Reuse the route once the old items fade

slides.p: During sleep the brain replays the day and moves memories from short-term holding into longer storage. An all-nighter before an exam undoes the studying; a nap after learning helps. Learn, sleep, test yourself the next day: that is the whole method in one line.

quiz.q: The forgetting curve shows that without review, most new material is lost…
a: Never; it's just hard to find
quiz.why: Ebbinghaus found the steepest loss in the first hours and days. Each review slows the next decline.

quiz.q: Which studying method produced better recall a week later?
a: Reading once and self-testing three times
quiz.why: Retrieval strengthens memory more than re-exposure, even though rereading feels more confident.

a: Studying one topic until it's perfect
Mixing related problem types in one session
quiz.why: Choosing the method each time is harder and transfers better to real use.

take: Review on a stretching schedule: 1, 3, 7, 14, 30 days.
Close the book and recall; testing beats rereading.
Mix topics, make it vivid, and sleep on it.

topics.title: Eight biases that run your decisions
topics.dek: The shortcuts the brain takes, and the questions that catch them

slides.p: We seek and remember what agrees with us and explain away what doesn't. It's why two people read the same report and both feel vindicated. The counter: ask what evidence would change your mind, then go looking for exactly that.

v.q: What would I expect to see if I were wrong?
v.by: the one question that catches most of them

slides.p: The first number sets the scale, even when it's random. In one study, spinning a wheel before guessing how many African countries are in the UN shifted the guesses toward the wheel's number. Prices, salaries and estimates all drift toward whatever was said first.

Vivid, recent and memorable things feel common. Plane crashes feel likelier than car crashes; shark attacks than falling coconuts. Whatever the news showed you this week feels like a trend. The counter is a base rate: how often does this actually happen per thousand, per year?

Losing $100 hurts about twice as much as gaining $100 feels good. So we hold losing stocks to avoid 'making it real', keep subscriptions we don't use, and accept bad deals framed as avoiding a loss. Reframe: if I didn't already own this, would I buy it today?

v.c: a loss weighs about twice as much as an equal gain

slides.p: Money and time already spent are gone whatever you do next, yet they drag us into finishing bad films, failing projects and dead relationships 'because we've come this far'. Only the future costs and benefits should count. The question: knowing what I know now, would I start this today?

We study the winners because they're the ones still around. The famous example: WWII analysts wanted to armor the parts of returning bombers that were full of holes, until Abraham Wald pointed out those planes came back; armor the places with no holes, where hit planes never returned.

items: where the survivors have no holes

slides.h: Dunning–Kruger and the expert's blind spot
slides.p: People with little skill in an area tend to overrate themselves because the skill needed to judge is the skill they lack; experts, knowing how much there is, often underrate themselves slightly. Confidence is a poor guide to competence, in yourself and in anyone selling you something.

slides.h: Hindsight, and how to beat all of it
slides.p: After the fact, everything looks like it was obvious, which stops us learning. Write down your prediction and your confidence before the result; review it after. A decision journal and a pre-mortem ('it's a year from now and this failed; why?') catch more biases than knowing their names.

items: Write the prediction and a confidence number first
Run a pre-mortem: assume it failed, list why
Decide, then revisit the journal later
Score the decision, not just the outcome

quiz.q: Wanting to finish a boring film 'because we paid for it' is…
quiz.why: The ticket money is gone either way. Only the next two hours should count in the decision.
The data came only from planes that survived. The missing planes, hit where the survivors had no holes, were the lesson.

quiz.q: The single question most useful against confirmation bias is…
a: What would I expect to see if I were wrong?
quiz.why: It forces you to name disconfirming evidence and then look for it.

take: Ask what you'd expect to see if you were wrong, and look for it.
Ignore sunk costs; count only what's ahead.
Write predictions down before the result; confidence isn't competence.
src: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow — Wikipedia

topics.title: Having the hard conversation
topics.dek: A structure for saying the difficult thing without starting a war

slides.h: Decide what the conversation is for
slides.p: Before you open your mouth, finish this sentence: 'By the end, I want us to…' If the honest answer is 'win' or 'make them feel bad', wait. Good goals are to be understood, to understand, to agree on a change, or to repair. Say the goal out loud at the start; it lowers the temperature.

items: 'I want us to find a way that works for both of us.'
'I want you to admit you were wrong.'
'I want to get this off my chest.'

slides.h: Pick the time and the place
slides.p: Not in front of others, not by text, not at the end of a long day, not when either of you is hungry or rushing. Ask for a time: 'Can we talk about the schedule tomorrow after lunch?' Giving notice lets the other person arrive ready instead of ambushed.

slides.h: Lead with what you saw, not what you concluded
slides.p: 'You left early three times this week' is an observation; 'you don't care about this team' is a verdict, and verdicts start fights. Describe the specific, checkable behavior. Then say its effect on you. Then stop and let them respond.

a: 'The report came in Thursday, not Tuesday'

slides.p: When I see [the specific thing], I feel [one word], because I need [the underlying need]. Would you be willing to [a concrete request]? It feels stiff at first. It also removes blame, names the real issue and asks for something doable instead of a change of character.

items: I feel… (one honest word, not 'that you…')
Would you be willing to… (specific, doable, soon)

slides.h: Listen to understand, then prove it
slides.p: After you've said your piece, the other person will say theirs, often heatedly. Don't rebut. Reflect it back: 'So from where you sit, the deadline moved without anyone telling you.' When they say 'yes, exactly', the defensive part of the conversation is usually over.

slides.h: Separate the facts from the story
slides.p: Most conflicts are two people telling different stories about the same facts. 'You didn't reply' is a fact; 'you were ignoring me' is a story. Ask for theirs: 'Help me see how it looked from your side.' You're not conceding; you're collecting the missing half.

items: A third story you both can hold

slides.h: When it gets hot, slow it down
slides.p: A raised voice, interruptions, 'you always', 'you never': the conversation has left the subject. Name it gently and pause. 'This matters to me too much to do badly; can we take ten minutes?' Come back when you said you would. A break is not a loss.

items: Name it, pause, set a time to resume

slides.p: Agreements that work are small, specific and dated: 'I'll send the agenda by Monday; you'll flag conflicts within a day.' Thank them for having the conversation. Then follow up in a week; the follow-up is what tells them it was real, and not just a mood.

items: A date to check how it's going
Actually check in on that date

quiz.q: Which opening is an observation rather than a verdict?
a: 'You looked at your phone while I was talking.'
quiz.why: It describes something both of you could see. Verdicts about character invite defence instead of discussion.

quiz.q: The best response when the other person pushes back heatedly is to…
a: Reflect back what they said until they confirm you've got it
quiz.why: Feeling understood defuses defensiveness. You can still disagree afterwards; you'll do it with the full picture.

quiz.q: A useful way to close a hard conversation is…
a: One small, specific, dated change each, and a check-in date
Agreeing never to discuss it again
quiz.why: Specific and dated agreements can be kept and checked; vague ones evaporate.

take: Name the goal first, pick a good moment, describe behavior rather than character.
When / I feel / because I need / would you be willing to.
Reflect before you rebut; end with one specific, dated change.
src: Difficult Conversations (Stone, Patton, Heen) — Harvard Negotiation Project
